title: Formulate
pitch: Your AI agent fills forms, explains jargon, and asks before it submits , powered by 12 WebMCP tools and a natural language data vault.
about_excerpt: Your AI agent fills forms, explains jargon, and asks before it submits , powered by 12 WebMCP tools and a natural language data vault. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration 67% of people abandon government forms at the first confusing field. We've all been there — staring at a 40-field form that asks for your CIN number, your GSTIN, your TDS rate, and nobody explains what any of it means. In India alone, 900 million voters interact with the Election Commission's Form 6. Millions fill out business registrations, insurance enrollments, and rental applications every year. Most people either pay someone to fill these forms or give up entirely. We asked: what if an AI agent could fill the form for you — explain every confusing field — and you just approve at the end? What it does Formulate is a WebMCP-powered form assistant with three parts: 1. Natural Language Data Vault You describe yourself in plain text: "My name is Mohammed, I work at TechVentures in Bengaluru, my PAN is ABCPM1234K." The vault extracts your data using pattern recognition — PAN format, Aadhaar format, phone numbers, PIN codes, email, employer, job title, city, state. No form to set up a form-filler. 2. Smart Form Engine Five real-world forms with 172 total fields: Rental Application (39 fields), Health Insurance Enrollment (27 fields), Small Business Registration (25 fields), Airtel Business Enterprise Registration (40 fields), and India's Election Commission Voter ID Form 6 (41 fields). Every confusing field has an inline plain-language explanation. 3. 12 WebMCP Tools Registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() — the agent calls structured tools instead of scraping the page: get_form_fields — reads the entire form structure fill_field — fills a text/number/date/phone field select_option — selects from a dropdown check_checkbox — toggles a checkbox explain_field — returns a plain-language explanation validate_form — checks for empty required fields get_form_progress — returns filled/total counts review_form — summarizes all values before submission clear_field — removes a value autofill_from_vault — checks what can be auto-filled apply_vault_suggestions — fills all matching fields from vault submit_form — requires human approval before proceeding How we built it Next.js 16 with App Router and TypeScript Tailwind CSS v4 with shadcn-style design tokens (2 colors: foreground and muted) WebMCP — supports both document.modelContext and navigator.modelContext for Chrome compatibility Pattern recognition vault — regex-based extraction for PAN, Aadhaar, GSTIN, CIN, Udyam, phone, email, PIN codes, plus keyword extraction for name, employer, job title, address Playwright — 30 end-to-end tests covering tool registration, field filling, validation, approval flow, and activity panel Vercel for deployment The execute function returns { content: [{ type: "text", text: "..." }] } per the Chrome WebMCP spec. Input parsing handles both JSON strings and parsed objects so it works regardless of how the host agent calls the tools. Challenges we faced The biggest challenge was WebMCP spec compliance. The API migrated from navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext in July 2026, and different hosts (Chrome vs ChatGPT) may use either surface. We had to support both. We also discovered that executeTool sends arguments as a JSON string in some hosts but a parsed object in others — so we added defensive input parsing. The natural language vault was tricky because names, cities, and job titles don't have fixed formats. We combined regex patterns for structured data (PAN, Aadhaar, GSTIN) with keyword-based extraction for unstructured data (name, employer, address), with confidence scoring to show users what was extracted and how sure we are. What we learned WebMCP changes the relationship between websites and AI agents from "scrape and guess" to "structured collaboration." A form that registers 12 tools gives the agent complete understanding of what's possible, what's required, and what needs human approval. That's fundamentally different from an agent trying to parse HTML and click buttons.
